question:
Barry wrote \(6\) different numbers, one on each side of \(3\) cards, and laid the cards on a table, as shown. The sums of the two numbers on each of the three cards are equal. The three numbers on the hidden sides are prime numbers. What is the average of the hidden prime numbers?

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_8_Q25_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The visible numbers are \(44,59,38\). The useful prime-number fact is that \(2\) is the only even prime: every larger even number has \(2\) as a factor besides \(1\) and itself.

If the common card sum were even, the hidden numbers opposite \(44\) and \(38\) would both be even primes. Both would have to equal \(2\), contradicting the condition that all six numbers are different. Therefore the common sum is odd.

Since \(59\) is odd, its hidden partner must be even to give an odd sum. That partner is consequently \(2\), making the common sum \(59+2=61\). The hidden numbers are therefore
\[
61-44=17,\qquad 61-59=2,\qquad 61-38=23.
\]
These are prime, and all six card numbers are different, so they satisfy the original conditions. Their average is
\[
\frac{17+2+23}{3}=\frac{42}{3}=\boxed{14},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
